H.R.5184 would replace the DOE manufactured-housing energy-standard regime in Energy Independence and Security Act section 413, retain a criteria-bound recommendation role to HUD, delete the specific section 413(c) penalty and give the May 31, 2022 rule at 87 FR 32728 no force or effect. Its whole mechanism is broader than withholding enforcement funds for one year. Under the retained section 17071 baseline, DOE is directed to establish standards by regulation after notice/comment and HUD consultation; the baseline uses the most recent IECC subject to its cost-effectiveness qualifications, supplies updating duties and caps its specific manufacturer civil penalty at one percent of retail list price. The bill replaces subsections (a) and (b) and strikes (c), rather than leaving that code-setting/update framework intact.
DOE may transmit recommendations to HUD; transmission is optional, but criteria for any recommendations are mandatory. Recommendations must be based on a cost-effectiveness determination taking life-cycle construction and operating costs into account, include estimates of initial purchase-price impact, and be developed considering factory-construction techniques/limitations, HUD climate zones, equivalent-or-improved energy-performance alternatives relative to the standard as proposed to be revised, and payback periods for added costs. These are analytical inputs required for proposed revisions, not established findings that homes or energy become cheaper. The bill does not require HUD to adopt every DOE recommendation. It does not repeal HUD’s separate section 5403(g) energy-standard duty or all HUD construction/safety and enforcement requirements. That selected HUD baseline retains cost-effective energy-performance standards, lowest total construction/operation costs, factory-design considerations and alternative practices. Removing the particular DOE penalty clause is not universal immunity from every housing law.
The specified 2022 rule supplies factory-stage manufactured-home standards, not a rule for every site-built home or every later household purchase. Its retained amendatory text distinguishes Tier 1 single-section homes and Tier 2 multi-section homes, with climate-zone requirements, prescriptive or overall-transmittance thermal-envelope paths, insulation and air-barrier installation, duct leakage, thermostat/control, service-hot-water, ventilation-fan and equipment-sizing provisions. Incorporated load/sizing materials and the source’s omitted graphic have not been independently inspected; this is not property-specific engineering or compliance approval. The rule’s technical categories are not replaced here with an invented retail-price tier cutoff.
The 2022 scope text contains an original May 31, 2023 compliance date, but the retained 2025 amendment replaces that scope with 60-day and 180-day clocks after publication of final enforcement procedures, respectively for the referenced single-section and multi-section categories. The old 2023 date is not presented as a current compliance deadline. No finding is made that final enforcement procedures were published, that a specific later calendar deadline applies, or that every separately issued later rule automatically disappears. The bill expressly targets the named 2022 final rule; this candidate does not independently resolve the complete current conformed regulatory position.
No actual recommendation, HUD adoption, home design, permit, penalty, compliance status, purchase price, energy bill, energy saving, emissions, construction volume, household benefit, causal outcome or motive is inferred. A Yea supports passing this whole role/criteria/penalty/rule package; a Nay opposes that exact package without proving opposition to affordability or energy performance generally. Infrastructure/Technology membership is an UNACCEPTED candidate proposal as an application of the existing direct physical-infrastructure/energy-system governance criterion. A competing boundary treats it as general private-housing regulation. Independent whole-mandate, legal, source and taxonomy review must resolve that mapping before acceptance or publication.
